items: TURN
Climbing-shoe repair through the gym desk
Illustrative seed pitch

slides.title: The rubber goes first.
items: The upper still fits.
Climbers break in a pair over months. Once the toe rubber thins, a familiar shoe can sit in a bag while its owner tries to find a repairer who will take it.
The gym already sees the shoe, the wear and the climber in the same visit.

slides.title: The desk takes the pair
items: Gym staff photograph the toe and heel and attach a numbered bag tag. The repairer accepts the job or sends a revised quote before cutting rubber.
A weekly collection consolidates the bags. The desk can look up the return date without calling the workshop.

slides.title: Keep the shape that fits
items: The cobbler removes worn rubber, checks the underlying rand and fits the agreed sole. A second person checks the bond and the pair number before dispatch.
The climber collects at the gym. A fit issue goes back under the same job number with a photograph and notes.

slides.title: One pair through the queue
items: MON
Desk intake and a photographed condition check. The climber approves the quote.
WED
Batch repair. A second check catches mismatched tags and unfinished edges.
FRI
Return to the original desk with care notes and a pickup message.

slides.title: A standard resole
items: Paid by the climber for a standard pair. Rand repairs are quoted separately after inspection.
$42 direct cost
Labor and materials cost $32, the gym receives $6 and bag handling costs $4. The remaining $26 funds fixed overhead and growth.

slides.title: Which route pays for itself?
items: Weekly contribution after a $260 fixed driver cost • illustrative dollars
Ten pairs cover the weekly route cost. At twenty pairs the route contributes $260 after that cost. The model excludes head-office overhead.

slides.title: Start with one climbing district
items: 24 gyms
Assume twelve pairs a week at each desk for 48 weeks. At $68 per pair, full adoption represents $940,032 in annual sales.
The route test
Sign neighboring desks before expanding the map. A gym that cannot fill a weekly bag joins a fortnightly pickup route.

slides.title: Why the gym holds the bag
items: Mail-in
Wide coverage, but every climber packs and tracks their own parcel.
Local cobbler
A direct relationship works for regulars. The climber still makes two separate trips.
Gym desk
A pickup on a normal climbing night. The workshop receives enough pairs to plan the batch.

slides.title: A bench lead and a route lead
items: Alex Tan / repair
Alex owns the bond check, rubber stock and training. The first workshop hire must complete a supervised batch before handling customer pairs.
Lou Finch / gym operations
Lou owns desk onboarding and weekly collections. Each gym gets one named contact and a shared list of jobs awaiting approval.

slides.title: Earn the next route
items: First 90 days
Open four desks. Follow the first hundred pairs from drop-off to collection.
By month six
Reach ten pairs a week per route and keep the proposed rework rate below 3%.
By month twelve
Operate twelve desks and renew at least three of the first four gym partnerships.

slides.title: Resole the first pair.
items: $620k seed
$260k equips two benches, $200k hires and trains repair staff, and $160k funds pickup routes and gym onboarding.
Twelve desks in twelve months. Illustrative company and financial model.
